strengths: The authors demonstrate that quantized discrete codebook encodings are more effective representations for continuous control, compared to alternative encodings, such as one-hot and label-based encodings.

The authors introduce DCWM: Discrete Codebook World Model, a model-based RL method which surpasses recent state-of-the-art algorithms, including TD-MPC2 and DreamerV3, on continuous control benchmarks.

The paper is well-written and explains all necessary background material in sufficient detail to understand the algorithm. While none of the individual components are novel, the experimental evaluation provides evidence that the proposed algorithmic details are critical for the success of model-based learning.
Strong paper with excellent methodology and solid experimental results.
Comparison with two SOTA baselines (Dreamer V3 and TD-MPC2) showing the method outperforms or matches baseline performance.
Additional experiments (sections 4.3, 4.4, 4.5) to understand how different variables affect performance, enhancing understanding of latent spaces in world model learning.
Paper's clarity is very good, with a great presentation of background and method.

Provides sufficient detail, such as discussion around the fixed FSQ codebook illustration in Figure 2 and extensive documentation of various tricks used to improve performance (lines 309, 352, 355, etc.).
Supplementary material is strong, with detailed extra information on method, environment, architecture, etc., and additional ablation experiments.

Results are significant, advancing the state of the art for model-based continuous control and contributing to understanding impacts of latent space encodings, losses, and stochasticity in modeling transition dynamics.

Method merits originality: cleverly combines prior work (consistency approach from TD-MPC2 and discrete encodings/cross entropy objective from Dreamer V3) and introduces novel elements such as codebook quantization.
The paper is well organized and easy to follow.
The description of the contribution to the article is simple and concise.
The ablation experiment is sufficient and persuasive.
The investigation into latent space design is valuable for the model-based RL community.
The experiments are informative, offering insights across multiple dimensions of the design.
Although similar ideas like the token-based world model were recently published, the proposed method seems computationally efficient, benefiting from the 'Finite Scalar Quantization' paper.
The paper first made the discrete latent space method work in continuous control tasks.
The paper writing is clear and easy to understand.
weaknesses: The paper misses a comparison with other approaches that are not based on the same embeddings ideas, such as MAMBA and Hungry hungry hippos (H3).

It is unclear how much of the demonstrated performance is due to the use of REDQ to reduce bias in TD learning, since the baseline does not use this method; a comparison with a version using standard one or two Q functions is needed.
The computational costs of the method are unclear; a more detailed comparison of training time and memory usage would be beneficial to understand practical implications.
The test for multi-task learning is missing; the authors should consider extending studies to multi-task learning and examine differences in codebooks between tasks.

In some Meta-World tasks, performance is comparable to TD-MPC2 with larger variance, suggesting a lack of robustness; a more detailed analysis of why the method does not consistently outperform TD-MPC2 across all tasks is needed.

The stochastic transition dynamics in the latent space could be better described; the current description lacks detail on how the categorical distribution is parameterized, how logits are generated, and how predicted probabilities are calibrated and lead to stable training.

The claim in the abstract that discrete latent spaces typically underperform in continuous control tasks needs specification; comparisons may be unfair due to differences in task types and planning components.
The distinction between label encoding and one-hot encoding is unclear and needs clarification.

Many elements in the methods section directly follow TD-MPC2, which may confuse non-expert readers regarding novelty; clearer differentiation is needed, e.g., regarding the ensemble of five critics and bootstrap sampling not being explicitly mentioned.
Algorithm 1 appears to be a standard procedure in model-based RL and could be moved to the appendix.
Clarify what is meant by "codebook encoding captures similarity between observations" and how this contrasts with one-hot encodings.
Explain why configuring the transition model to accept label and one-hot encodings resulted in the agent being unable to learn.
Explain the sentence about the codebook being configured with b = 2 channels and the label encoding incorrectly assuming an ordinal structure; how does the hyperparameter b affect label encoding?
In Line 514, why is |C| = 2^4 for L = [5,3] when it is claimed that |C| = \prod L_i in Line 224?
Provide additional experiments on more tasks such as ManiSkill2/Myosuite and on more base algorithms such as DreamerV3.
Conduct head-to-head comparisons by replacing the latent space in DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 with the proposed approach; explain why this was not done.
Compare FSQ and VQ (dictionary learning) methods.
Provide numerical analysis to support the claim that codebook encoding is more computationally efficient, given that it only outperforms one-hot encoding in one task in Figure 6.
The paper lacks comparisons with more advanced baselines like EfficientZero-V2.
The authors didn't test the proposed method with visual inputs, weakening the paper.
